title: Anaconda acquires Enkrypt AI, folding red-teaming and MCP scanning into its enterprise platform
subtitle: The August 4 deal brings pre-deployment red-teaming across 300+ attack categories, NIST and EU AI Act compliance automation, and a scanner that found 143,000 vulnerabilities across 25,000 MCP servers in the last two months.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anaconda announced on August 4 that it has acquired Enkrypt AI for an undisclosed sum. Enkrypt's platform provides pre-deployment red-teaming across more than 300 attack categories, runtime guardrails, and compliance automation aligned to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act. In the two months before the acquisition, Enkrypt's scanner examined more than 268,000 tools across 25,000 Model Context Protocol servers and found more than 143,000 vulnerabilities, affecting 73 percent of the servers scanned. Enkrypt's research team has previously red-teamed models from Anthropic, Mistral, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and DeepSeek — and reports finding exploitable attack categories in every one.

The mechanism is worth unpacking. MCP — the protocol Anthropic released in November 2024 and that most agent frameworks now use to expose tools to LLMs — is the connective tissue of production AI systems. Every MCP server exposes some set of tools (search, file access, database queries, API calls) to whichever model is calling it. When Enkrypt reports that 73 percent of scanned MCP servers have vulnerabilities, the implication is that the majority of production agent deployments today expose attack surfaces the operators may not know exist. Anaconda buying that capability is a bet that scanning agentic infrastructure will become a table-stakes IT function, on the same footing as scanning container images or dependency trees.

The consolidation trend is real. Anaconda acquired Kilo Code in July for orchestration and agentic engineering; Enkrypt brings the security layer. Snyk acquired Probely earlier in the year to extend into runtime AI security. Datadog and Palo Alto Networks have both launched AI-security modules in 2026. The market is coalescing around a small number of platforms that combine model observability, prompt-injection defense, MCP scanning, and compliance evidence — the way DevSecOps consolidated around a few vendors between 2018 and 2022. Enterprises that build on top of any of these platforms are signing multi-year lock-in trades that will look, five years from now, a lot like the current cloud provider commitments.

For learners: the shape of AI-security tooling gives you a checklist for evaluating any agent system you build or use. Does it have pre-deployment red-teaming across a documented attack taxonomy? Does it produce runtime telemetry — and can that telemetry be replayed for post-incident review? Does it generate compliance artifacts mapped to a specific framework (NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001)? If any of these are missing, the system is running on trust rather than evidence. In 2026 that is still tolerable inside research prototypes; by 2027 it will not be tolerable inside anything customer-facing. Learn the vocabulary now — auditors and buyers will expect it fluently within the year.
